about: Externally observed metadata for the B0 run. Not harness output.
status: measured — file level only, and NOT part of the H1 decision

git.commit_note: Run after the file-level metric and the B0 query/rate-limit/chunk-id corrections landed.

reproducibility.why: Every other figure in this repository can be regenerated by re-reading files under results/. This one cannot. It queries GitHub's live code-search index, which re-crawls and re-ranks, so re-running it is a fresh measurement rather than a reproduction. The recorded numbers are what that index returned on 2026-07-31.
reproducibility.consequence: It is deliberately excluded from the generated-artifact drift check, whose guarantee only holds while the generator is a pure function of committed bytes. See docs/en/Honesty_Constraints.md §11.

unit_of_retrieval.why: GitHub's code search returns a path, a matched fragment, and character offsets within that fragment. Verified against a live response: there is no line number anywhere in the payload. B0 therefore has no chunk-level result. Synthesising one — by expanding a file to all its chunks, or by locating the fragment in our own copy — would credit the baseline with a precision it does not have, in whichever direction the mapping happened to fall.
unit_of_retrieval.comparison_basis: The harness computes file-level Recall/MRR/nDCG for every arm from data it already records, so B0 is compared in its own unit against arms measured the same way.

corpus.note: GitHub searches its own index of the default branch, not the pinned commit 414f0513 that every other arm was evaluated against. The two corpora are close but not identical, and this asymmetry cannot be removed — it is what querying an external service means.

execution.command: PYTHONPATH=... uv run python -m dcode_eval.run --baseline B0 --questions apps/eval/src/dcode_eval/questions/data/questions.jsonl --output results/eval-b0-2026-07-31 --k 5 --repo-id 2543893e-0965-4be7-ac45-5a8e38600bc0
execution.rate_limit_note: GitHub's code-search endpoint allows 10 requests/minute authenticated. An earlier version of this baseline assumed 30/min and slept 2s, which would have tripped 403 partway through a 33-question suite and recorded the remaining questions as zeros indistinguishable from real results.
execution.token_scopes: none — public-repo code search needs no scopes; the token only raises the rate limit

comparison_file_recall_at_5.note: Derived from the recorded retrieved_files of results/eval-h1-repeat3-2026-07-31 (mean of its three repeats). No baseline was re-executed to produce these; the metric is a pure function of retrieval output that run already wrote. That run's own artifacts were left untouched.

fairness: The first attempt scored 0.253 with 14 empty results and L3 at exactly 0.000, and that was OUR fault, not GitHub's. The keyword extractor sent 'Explain' as a required search term — GitHub ANDs every term, and all 17 expansion questions open with that word. Reporting an L3 zero produced that way would have been a strawman.

The extractor was rewritten to favour identifiers (backticked symbols, snake_case, CamelCase, dotted paths) and to send at most three terms, which is the query a competent user of code search would type. B0 improved to 0.308 suite recall and L3 0.111. The baseline was made stronger deliberately, which costs us margin.

12 of 33 questions still return nothing. That is a genuine property of keyword search against natural-language architecture questions, not an artefact of the query builder — the remaining queries are identifier-led and short.
Beating a keyword baseline is not a strong claim and should not be presented as one. B0 is a control that establishes the floor, not a rival.
limitations: Not in the H1 decision. h1_report reads B2/B3/B4 only, and B0 has no chunk-level result to contribute even if it were.
Single run, no repeats. Unlike the current H1 snapshot, no variance is measured here.
GitHub indexes the default branch and may not index every file of a repository.
